description: "We are team SHARK working on the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, bringing together our backgrounds in space science and interactive design to build an engaging learning experience."
summary: Outpost Commander is a browser game where students run a 4-person lunar or Martian outpost for 30 sols. Each sol, players spend 8 crew-hours on solar panels, life-support recyclers, greenhouse beds, or radiation shielding. The systems depend on each other. If power fails, recycling fails, and then oxygen and water run out. A forecast shows each coming event, such as a dust storm, solar particle event, hull leak, or equipment failure, so players learn to plan ahead. The Moon and Mars play differently. The Moon has a 14-day night, and Mars has weak sunlight and dust storms. We built it so young learners feel real engineering trade-offs without needing advanced math. It runs on any phone or laptop with no install.
details: What it does and how it works Outpost Commander is a browser game where the player is the commander of a 4-person Moon or Mars outpost for 30 sols (days). Each sol, the player has 8 crew-hours to spend on four things: solar panels, life-support recyclers, greenhouse beds, or radiation shielding. The game simulates battery power, oxygen, water, food, radiation dose and crew health. The systems depend on each other. If power fails, the recycler and greenhouse go offline, and then oxygen and water run out. Random events include dust storms, solar particle events, hull leaks and equipment failures. A forecast shows each event one sol ahead, so players can plan. The player wins by keeping the crew alive to sol 30. Benefits Makes engineering trade-offs tangible and fun. Works on any phone or laptop with no install and no login. Each run is different because events are random. Moon and Mars play differently. Intended impact We want students to understand that real missions succeed or fail on trade-offs, not on a single big idea. Players learn systems thinking, why backups matter, and why radiation and power planning are central to living off Earth. It can be used in classrooms or at home. Tools and technology HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, hosted on GitHub Pages. No external libraries or servers. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant to generate the game code and text, and our team reviewed it. NASA data used NASA Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (crew O₂, water and food needs), NASA MSL/Curiosity RAD (Mars surface radiation of about 0.67 mSv/day), NASA lunar radiation data (about 1.37 mSv/day), and the NASA Moon and Mars Fact Sheets (lunar night length, Mars sunlight at about 43% of Earth's). We simplified and rounded these values for gameplay. Creativity The game turns a systems-engineering problem into a simple resource game. The one-sol-ahead forecast mimics real NASA space weather warnings. Moon and Mars have different challenges: a long lunar night versus weak sunlight and dust storms. What our team considered Keeping the game simple enough for young players while keeping the dependencies between systems real. Making it accessible, with a phone-friendly layout. Balancing difficulty so it is challenging but winnable. Being clear about what is simplified, and crediting the NASA sources and our use of AI.
